---
title: "MIMO & joint modal identification"
---

The [closing-the-loop](closing-the-loop.qmd) page fits one transfer function per
degree of freedom. A suspension is not one transfer function — it is a coupled,
multi-input / multi-output (MIMO) system whose degrees of freedom **share the same
resonances**. The longitudinal, pitch and yaw responses of a single stage all ring at
the same modal frequencies; what differs between elements is how strongly each
mode couples in and out. This page is the theory home for the joint fit that uses
that structure — the parametric step on top of the ordinary Pintelon–Schoukens
measurement that the [worked example 09](../examples/09-rank1-modal-mimo.qmd) and the
[real-SRM example 10](../examples/10-srm-hsts.qmd) run end-to-end.

## Shared poles, coupled elements

For an $n_y \times n_u$ mechanical system (here $n_y$ sensors, $n_u$ actuators), every
element $G_{ij}(s)$ of the response matrix is a ratio of polynomials that **share one
denominator** — the characteristic polynomial whose roots are the modal poles. Pintelon
& Schoukens call this the **common-denominator model** (§6.6):

$$
G(s;\theta) = \frac{B(s;\theta)}{A(s;\theta)}
            = \frac{\sum_r B_r\, s^r}{\sum_r a_r\, s^r},
\qquad B_r \in \mathbb{R}^{n_y \times n_u},\quad a_r \in \mathbb{R}.
$$

The **scalar** denominator $A$ carries the shared poles (the modes); the
**matrix** numerator $B$ carries the coupling, one free polynomial per I/O element.
This is the book's default because the rational $B/A$ form has good linear-least-squares
starting values and avoids the local minima of a partial-fraction parameterization.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why this package fits a rank-1 modal model instead

At MIMO scale the free-per-element numerator $B$ has enough freedom to absorb pole
errors — the shared denominator drifts while the numerators compensate, and the modal
frequencies come out biased. For a proportionally-damped, reciprocal mechanical structure
the residue of each mode is **rank one**, so the physics can be parameterized directly and
that freedom removed. `mimo_modal.Rank1ModalModel` implements

$$
G_{ij}(s) = \sum_{k=1}^{n_\text{modes}}
   \frac{\varphi_{k,i}\,\psi_{k,j}}{s_n^2 + b_k\, s_n + a_k},
\qquad s_n = \frac{s}{s_\text{ref}},
$$

with shared poles $(a_k, b_k)$ and a **rank-1 real residue** $R_k = \varphi_k\,\psi_k^{\!\top}$
per mode — a sensor mode shape $\varphi_k$ times an actuator mode shape $\psi_k$. All the
coupling lives in the mode shapes, not in the residue rank. Frequencies are normalized
by $s_\text{ref} = 2\pi\,\text{median}(f)$ so the high-order evaluation stays conditioned.
(If the residues were genuinely full-rank — non-reciprocal, non-proportional damping — the
common-denominator $B/A$ would be the correct fallback. For LIGO suspensions the rank-1
modal form is both correct and better conditioned.)
:::

The pole $\lambda_k$ (a root of $s_n^2 + b_k s_n + a_k$, de-normalized) maps to the
familiar modal parameters by

$$
f_{0,k} = \frac{|\lambda_k|}{2\pi}, \qquad
Q_k = \frac{|\lambda_k|}{-2\,\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda_k}.
$$

## The estimator — sample-ML, no matrix inverse

The measurement is the ordinary campaign: drive each actuator in turn with a periodic
multisine (P&S's robust method, $n_\text{exp} = n_u$ uncorrelated experiments), observe
$M$ steady-state periods, and DFT each period on the excited-line grid. From the periods,
per experiment $l$ and excited bin $k$, come the **sample-mean** input/output spectra
$\hat U^{[l]},\hat Y^{[l]}$ and their **sample covariance** $\hat C_Z^{[l]}$ (the
period-to-period scatter — the same period-variance machinery the SISO path uses).

The fit minimizes a **sample-ML equation-error cost** directly on those spectra:

$$
V(\theta) = \sum_{l}\sum_{k\in\mathbb{K}}
   e^{\mathsf H}\!\left(\hat C_\varepsilon^{[l]}\right)^{-1}\! e,
\qquad
e = \hat Y^{[l]}(k) - G(s_k;\theta)\,\hat U^{[l]}(k)
  = \big[\,I,\;-G(s_k;\theta)\,\big]\,\hat Z^{[l]}(k),
$$

with the residual covariance projected through the same $[\,I,-G\,]$:

$$
\hat C_\varepsilon^{[l]} = \big[\,I,\;-G\,\big]\,\hat C_Z^{[l]}\,\big[\,I,\;-G\,\big]^{\mathsf H}.
$$

Two properties follow from this structure:

- **It is unbiased in closed loop** (given the reference). The weighting
  $\hat C_\varepsilon$ carries the noise on both $Y$ and the measured plant input $U$ and
  their cross-covariance — an errors-in-variables fit. Because the injected multisine is
  the reference and the sample mean over periods is the noise-free reference-driven response,
  the fit needs no controller model: the loop is part of the plant that maps drive to
  response. (This is the same reference-based cancellation the [SISO closed-loop
  mode](closing-the-loop.qmd#identifying-in-closed-loop-controller-aware) uses.)
- **It never inverts the FRF.** The cost fits the raw $\hat Y,\hat U$ spectra, so there is
  no $\hat G = Y\!\cdot\!X^{-1}$ step. The per-bin matrix inverse is ill-conditioned
  at the resonances (the drive monitors are small there); the equation-error
  weighting handles resonances without it. This is why the parametric fit predicts
  cleanly through the peaks where the nonparametric $Y\!\cdot\!X^{-1}$ overlay scatters —
  see example 09's through-resonance figure. The recovered $\hat G$ is kept only as a
  nonparametric **overlay for validation** and to seed starting values.

The minimization is Gauss–Newton on a pseudo-Jacobian (the weighting is $\theta$-dependent,
so the step keeps the $\tfrac12(\partial\hat C_\varepsilon/\partial\theta)$ term); the model
supplies an **analytic** $\partial G/\partial\theta$ that feeds both the step and the CRB.
`mimo_fit.MIMOModalEstimator.fit` is the implementation.

## Starting values without an oracle

The fit is seeded from the **data**, not a prior. `mimo_fit.find_modes` searches the summed
FRF power $\sum_{ij}|\hat G_{ij}(f)|^2$ for prominent, well-separated peaks (with a
prominence gate and a minimum modal separation), estimates each peak's $Q$ from its width,
and returns a mode set and count — a data-driven **model order**. Those seed the poles;
`init_residues` then solves a linear least squares for the rank-1 shapes. Because the modes
are found from the recovered FRF, the recovery is the same whether the design prior was
right or badly wrong — the property example 09 demonstrates and example 10 relies on to fit
the real SRM blind.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Do not over-count modes
Seeding more poles than the data resolves collapses the shared denominator into
near-cancelling pairs and makes the Fisher matrix singular. `find_modes` counts distinct,
resolvable peaks; a genuine near-degeneracy is handled by the tools in the last two
sections, not by adding a coincident pole.
:::

## Uncertainty: the CRB on every mode

The parameter covariance is the practical Cramér–Rao bound from the Gauss–Newton Hessian,

$$
\mathrm{Cov}(\hat\theta) \approx \big(2\,\mathrm{Re}\,J^{\mathsf H} J\big)^{-1},
$$

built by `mimo_fisher_matrix` / `mimo_parameter_covariance` from the analytic Jacobian
weighted by the campaign covariance. Propagating $\mathrm{Cov}(\hat\theta)$ through the
pole map gives a per-mode $(f_0, Q)$ uncertainty (`modal_uncertainty`) and a per-bin FRF
envelope (`frf_band`). The worst-parameter fractional uncertainty
`modal_frac_uncertainty` is the MIMO analogue of the SISO stop criterion — the DONE test
the iterative loop (`mimo_iterate.iterate_mimo`) drives toward.

::: {.callout-note}
## How many periods?
For the sample covariance to give a trustworthy CRB, P&S require
$\text{dof} \ge n_y + 8$ degrees of freedom (roughly, periods/blocks). For a 6-DoF
suspension that is $\text{dof} \ge 14$. Fewer periods can still converge, but the reported
error bars are not yet trustworthy — a real constraint on how short the campaign can be, and
one the feasibility gate requires be stated with the number rather than hand-waved.
:::

## Sizing the measurement — resolution from the ringdown

The frequency resolution is not guessed; it is derived from the prior. A mode $(f_0, Q)$ has
linewidth $\Gamma = f_0/Q$ and ringdown $\tau = Q/(\pi f_0)$. To resolve $Q$ (not just
$f_0$) the fit needs several bins across each resonance, $df \le \Gamma / (\text{a few
bins})$; since $df = 1/T$, that sets a minimum record length $T \gtrsim Q/f_0$.
`design.resolution.recommend_resolution` turns the prior modes into the concrete
$(n_\text{fft}, df, n_\text{transient})$ campaign knobs. Resolution and record length are
**controlled variables set from the math**, not fixed limits — see
[Fisher & excitation](fisher.qmd) for the CRB behind them.

## Near-degenerate modes: spatial vs frequency

Two modes at nearly the same frequency are the case where it is easiest to mistake a
modeling choice for a physical wall. There are two genuinely different situations, and the
feasibility gate requires distinguishing them:

- **Spatial doublet.** If the plant block-diagonalizes into orthogonal DOF subspaces (a
  suspension whose dynamics split into, say, the $\{L,P,V\}$ and $\{T,R,Y\}$ planes), two
  modes coincident in frequency can live in different blocks. A single shared-pole fit
  collapses the pair — one pole set forced across two orthogonal modes makes $J^{\mathsf H}J$
  ill-conditioned — but that is a **parameterization** artifact, not a data limit.
  `mimo_fit.fit_block_decoupled` fits each block alone, where only one of the pair appears,
  and recovers both with no finer $df$ and no super-resolution. This is the
  0.67 Hz doublet resolved in [example 10](../examples/10-srm-hsts.qmd).
- **Frequency near-degeneracy.** Two modes in the same block, separated by $\Delta f$
  below a linewidth, are a true frequency-resolution question. It is still not a wall:
  parametric ML super-resolves, and the CRB gives the cost — the required budget grows as
  a steep but finite power of $\Gamma/\Delta f$. Compute it and report the record length or
  SNR that resolves the pair; a one-bin / one-linewidth (Rayleigh) limit should never be
  quoted against a parametric fit. See
  [*Resolvability of two modes*](fisher.qmd#when-are-two-modes-resolvable).

## Worked examples

- [**09 — Joint MIMO modal identification**](../examples/09-rank1-modal-mimo.qmd): the full
  step run on a six-mode teaching plant under closed-loop damping — through-resonance
  recovery, the data-driven peak-pick init, and the per-mode CRB.
- [**10 — SRM modal identification**](../examples/10-srm-hsts.qmd): the same step on the real

## References

Pintelon & Schoukens, *System Identification: A Frequency Domain Approach*, 2nd ed.,
Wiley-IEEE Press, 2012 — §6.6 (common-denominator and rank-1 residue models), §12.3
(joint MIMO sample-ML fit, pseudo-Jacobian, CRB, model validation). The literal step-2
procedure and its mapping onto this package are recorded in
`.llm/pintelon-schoukens-mimo-fit.md`.
